answer.rationale:
The tempting move is the one the memory most directly endorses: memory_c2 says the low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply with quick onboarding, and their quote alone satisfies the 18% mandate. That is exactly why it deserves scrutiny rather than deference. The line is at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days; a primary-source migration in that window converts a cost win into an availability bet, and memory_c2 is a single consolidated summary with the qualifying detail stripped out (what volume share, what component criticality, whether the cost delta survived the full cycle, whether any quality or return cost showed up later). I want the archived source for memory_c2 to see whether 'quick onboarding' meant a primary cutover under load or a partial/second-source ramp, and the source for memory_c4 because negotiation leverage is the action I intend to spend the cycle on and I need to know whether the benchmarking that moved the incumbent was on a comparable component and volume, or a one-off.

Intent: negotiate_terms with the incumbent, using the low-cost vendor's quote as documented benchmark leverage (the mechanism memory_c4 credits) and multi-year volume structure (memory_c6) as the cost lever, while memory_c1 indicates the incumbent relationship holds delivery stable through renewal. I am scoping it as a small guarded test rather than a broad commitment: a short bridge or narrow-term deal that closes the 14-day cliff and captures part of the mandate without locking a multi-year price before the low-cost vendor is qualified. add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right structural answer to the single-point-of-failure exposure but does not address the spend mandate this cycle and does not beat the expiry clock; defer_decision (memory_c5) applied to a non-critical renewal and does not transfer to a primary contract feeding a line with no buffer.

Downstream value risk: the 18% mandate is a cost-only objective, and satisfying it by the single cheapest path pushes risk off the sourcing ledger and onto delivery commitments, line continuity, and eventually customers who bear stockouts or quality regressions. That tradeoff should be named explicitly to finance rather than absorbed silently. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving this cycle: whether the low-cost vendor's cost advantage holds at our current volume and criticality, and whether their capacity survives a shortage. If verification shows memory_c2's win came from a genuine primary cutover on a comparable part with sustained cost and quality, switch_primary_vendor becomes materially more credible and I would revisit; if it shows a partial or non-critical scope, the case for treating it as a qualified second source next cycle strengthens instead.
